commenti.body:
No argument with you on this one. John is not a likable guy by modern standards, and his “romance” with Madeline is the kind of once sided, male centered stories of “love” that I guess were common at that time. I recall a scene where he’s pleading with Madeline that he loves her, as if that fact alone requires her to reciprocate. And the age gaps in all the Hitchcock relationships are often quite large.

As a viewer, It’s one of those things I notice when watching older films but I generally just go with the flow to enjoy the film as it is. But I was definitely wondering on my last rewatch of Vertigo is John was intended to being as pitiful a character as he came across being.

Ugh, your take is so immature. I’m not sure what the issue is - is it a generational thing? Why is it so important that someone be a “good” guy or a “bad” guy? Is it due to a steady diet of Disney that you have been robbed of your ability to see anything else in a film besides an allegory and whether or not the main character is a good guy or bad guy? It saddens me that you are unable to watch one of the greatest films ever made and grasp the complexity of the plot, the interaction with the music (scored by one of the greatest music composers who ever lived) as well as the unique cinematography and even the graphics (designed by Saul Bass, one of the greatest title sequence designers who ever lived). Maybe when you grow up a little you can rewatch the film and take it for what it is rather than needing the characters to be good or bad. Btw, Madeline isn’t a good person either. Gavin isn’t good, none of the them are “good” people. Hey, here’s another thing that might disturb you: most people are not good. Go watch the new Pixar film so you won’t be so disturbed by characters with nuance.

I feel like you're spending more time judging the characters as people than going along with the plot and its twists. 

I'm not saying don't have an opinion of a character. It's Hitchcock, though. It's about the psychology of characters, not their worth, as they are placed in uncomfortable, dare I say, thrilling situations, like hanging off a bell tower 

tl;dr Hitchcock = psychological thriller, not emotional drama. Some other director, different thing.

They're both pretty bad, and horrible for each other. Red flags all around on both sides of that relationship, lol.


Midge: also not great. She's a prototypical NiceGuy(tm) sort of character. 


They're all pretty disturbed, but it's all so brilliantly constructed to sweep us away, particularly the score by Bernard Herring. He also did the score for Taxi Driver, another film that offers a romance fantasy  that anyone with any distance from the characters can tell you is not likely to have a real-life hollywood ending.

I'd recommend OP never watch "Rashomon" or anything Bergman if she discountenances Vertigo all together. Definitely strange things to focus on. That said, I'm not a particularly big fan of Hitchcock myself when it comes to his narratives but for less strange reasons. Surprisingly, [Tarantino](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sayqh91OF4I) has an clip where he echoes some of my thoughts.

I mean for a film where a romance is extremely central, a completely unlikable, unromantic lead really hurts the buy in.  I simply cannot fathom how Judy sees anything in him at all, and the one sided depiction doesn't help.

Yes, it is quite unfortunate. My view is that the movie does not endorse his creepy behavior, but it still makes for an uncomfortable watch. No denying Vertigo's technical mastery or quality of the storytelling. More the story itself is the issue.

Romance is not Hitchcock's strong suit, to put it lightly. Despite that many of the relationships in his movies are intended to be toxic, they often don't land with me in the way I imagine they were intended to. For reasons that you and other commenters have addressed.

Interesting parallel with Citizen Kane. Two holders of the "greatest movie ever" title (whatever that means) are in-depth character studies of tortured men who abuse the women in their lives.

Bernard Herrmann, I guess Herring is a common iPhone audotcorrect 🤣 I agree all the main characters are a little off, but it wouldn’t be half as good if they weren’t. And the score is one of the most iconic and influential scores ever.
Aargh! Yes, autocorrect (but on android). Thanks for noting that! And i agree on all points.

"John is a terrible person." Isn't it more complicated than that? In any case, what does it matter if a protagonist is good or bad? What should this have any bearing whatsoever on whether a film has cinematic merit?
[removed]

I have some information for you which you may not like: nobody is perfect. We all have flaws, obsessions, things that press our buttons (for better or for worse). Some of us may voluntarily do the 'wrong' thing just once, others will have a bad experience not of their making - both of those examples may shape the rest of our lives.

You seem to want these characters to be perfect and you are upset that they aren't. They are flawed characters, and that's fine.

Your criticisms show that you have missed the whole point of the movie and in order to justify your apparent dislike of it you are resorting to some bad takes and general nit-picking.

When you're in the correct frame of mind I would recommend reading or watching a few detailed analyses of the movie, maybe then you will start to appreciate it for it it is. There's plenty out there.

It's a great movie. The most interesting aspect of it is how the real Madeline is Judy, but then Judy ends up having to become then perfect imitation of Madeline but never quite living up to her. 


It's mentally fucked in a great way. How she can't live up to the person she invented

John is a disturbed and melancholy individual. His close encounter with death triggers in him an obsessive pulse that leads him to be drawn to the mysterious line between life and death, symbolized by his Vertigo.

Midge represents life. She represents the here and now. The Apollonian way of being. Madeline represents death. She (he's led to believe) is possessed by the spirit of a suicidal woman. She holds the secrets of the grave.

Through these characters, the film explores obsession, depression, urges from the unconscious, the desire for something more than physical reality, the impulse to recreate life through art, etc.

Now imagine a film in which John is a fully functioning and rational individual. He takes Madeline to the hospital after saving her. He respects her privacy. He does not meddle in her life (to respect his friend's marriage). Instead, he dates Midge.

It would be a bland and sterile movie where good characters behave in a good, exemplary way. Would that be interesting?

I don't think it's generational. OP is probably a teenager who's just dipping his toes into movies. The idea that "the main character shouldn't behave in a reprehensible way" is clearly taken from straight "good vs evil" kind of stories, which he's probably being mainly exposed to until now. That's my hope at least.
Good point, well made

Just to clarify, I've watch Vertigo at least 3 times, it is without doubt a masterpiece of cinema and I regard Hitchcock as one of the best directors of all time. 

It just struck me, on this particular rewatch, that we're supposed to root for John and feel sorry for him being deceived, but it's hard to do that when he behaves in so unlikeable a way. He's the protagonist, but he feels more like an anti-hero. 

I sympathise with Judy - used and abused by every man she's ever met - a lot more. And of course the real Madeline - already dead and tossed out of a bell tower!

As an aside, Gavin must've been a lot stronger then he looked to drag a dead body all the way up there and chuck her out. Or is the suggestion he drugged her and she was alive when he pushed her?

I don’t think Hitchcock makes any excuses for him. Scotty is obsessive, voyeuristic, controlling, perpetually chasing the past, while very much in the grip of mommy issues.  And then it’s very vertigo-inducing to recognize that cycles of those exact masculine impulses have been shaping the world for thousands of years.

> I know, it's Hitchcock's "magnum opus".

> But John is a terrible person.

...yes? I don't know why a director's magnum opus would necessarily have to have virtuous characters.

In fact, part of the effectiveness of Vertigo is that it casts James Stewart, who had played a lot of likable "everyman" sort of characters, as someone who turns out to be pretty dispicable. Hitchcock is deliberately playing with his audience's expectations. Our discomfort with Scottie's actions—indeed, our implication in them too, as the audience "gazing" upon Madeleine in the same way Scottie gazes upon her—is precisely the point of the film.

> It just struck me, on this particular rewatch, that we're supposed to root for John and feel sorry for him being deceived,

I don't think we're supposed to root for him at all. At least, not once you've seen the whole film from start to finish. But you're right in the sense that Hitchcock's positioning of Scottie as the protagonist leads the audience to sympathize with him at first. That's why his later behavior is such a rug pull for the audience.

>John should've jumped out that window

Not sure to what window you refer.  But the last shot in the movie is of Scottie on the parapet of the bell tower.  (He has just seen "Madeleine" fall again.  He has just heard the nun say "I heard voices" and "May God have mercy.")  He is in the same posture he is in during his fall in his dream.  Hint, hint.  No, I do not claim Scottie does fall from the parapet; I also don't claim he doesn't.  I claim the movie leaves him in a state of fascinating, beautiful, dynamic equilibrium--a visual metaphor of his state throughout the movie.

I have seen this movie many times and I don't think I have ever concluded that Scottie is a terrible person.   I am unsure how that judgment could help me enjoy the movie or express my feelings about it.  Instead, I have drawn many other conclusions, rational and irrational, about him and the movie.

This "John is a terrible person" criticism seems to miss much in the movie.  But you are free to like and dislike any movie you please for whatever reason you please.
